newsitem.title: FRANCE: MEPs demand better provisions on free movement.
newsitem.headline: MEPs demand better provisions on free movement.

text.p: The European Parliament demanded improvements on Wednesday to a package of proposals designed to make it easier for people to move freely around the European Union single market.
MEPs adopted three draft directives proposed by the European Commission in July 1995 after parliament took it to court for failure to take action in this area.
But they asked for a series of amendments to improve the texts.
The first directive proposes abolishing identity controls on people crossing the border between different EU countries -- COM(95)347.
The second concentrates on removing restrictions which prevent EU workers and their families from moving to or residing in another member state -- COM(95)348.
The last gives third country nationals who are lawfully resident in a member state the right to travel to any of the other 14 -- COM(95)346.

To parliament's annoyance, the Commission's proposals make the removal of these border restrictions dependent on the introduction of accompanying measures on asylum applications, visas for third country nationals and controls on people crossing the EU's external frontiers.
Neither the three related draft directives nor the flanking measures can come into effect unless they obtain the unanimous backing of the Council, an outcome which MEPs believe is far from assured.

While acknowledging that the flanking measures are important, parliament introduced amendments making it clear that delays in bringing in these measures cannot be used as a pretext for not abolishing border controls by the December 31, 1996 deadline.
MEPs insisted all people legally resident in the Union, including non-EU citizens, should be allowed to cross the EU's internal borders without having to produce a passport or visa.

They also reminded the member states that they are bound by the European Convention on Human Rights and should not expel to another member state third country nationals who have a right to their protection.
